h1: St. John's travel, stays & events guide
heroText: St. John's works best as a base in Canada when you anchor days around Signal Hill, George Street and Quidi Vidi. Use those sights to understand the city's history, street life and visitor rhythm. St. John's International Airport handles the main arrival flow, so hotel choice should balance the centre, transfer time and day-trip plans.

stayOverview: Start with City centre for the easiest first St. John's stay, then compare Old Town and Waterfront when price, nightlife, quieter evenings or transfer timing matter more than being beside every major sight.
hotelIntro: St. John's hotel choice is mostly about repeat journeys: use City centre for sightseeing, Old Town for a different local base, and Waterfront or Airport area when views, parking, airport timing or longer stays matter.
rentalCars: Do not rent a car for central St. John's unless parking and traffic are part of the plan; use one mainly for regional day trips.

travelTips.title: Best base
travelTips.text: Choose City centre for a first stay because it keeps main sights, restaurants and practical local movement close.

travelTips.title: Airport timing
travelTips.text: Leave extra time for St. John's International Airport, especially for early flights, late arrivals, traffic or unfamiliar transfer routes.

travelTips.title: Local movement
travelTips.text: Plan each day in clusters around Signal Hill and George Street so transfers do not consume the best sightseeing hours.

travelTips.title: Day trips
travelTips.text: Keep one flexible slot for nearby routes from St. John's, checking weather, transport and opening hours before committing.

history.text: When 1500 English reinforcements arrived in late 1697, they found rubble where the town and fortifications had stood.

source.label: Wikipedia: St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador

history.text: The earliest record of the location appears as São João on a Portuguese map by Pedro Reinel in 1519.

source.label: Wikipedia: St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador

history.text: When the English mariner John Rut visited St. John's in 1527, he found Norman, Breton and Portuguese ships in the harbour.

source.label: Wikipedia: St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador

history.label: 16th century
history.text: A series of expeditions to St. John's by Portuguese from the Azores took place in the early 16th century, and by 1540, French, Spanish and Portuguese ships crossed the Atlantic annually to fish the waters off the Avalon Peninsula.

source.label: Wikipedia: St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador

history.text: On 5 August 1583, an English Sea Dog, Sir Humphrey Gilbert, claimed the area as England's first overseas colony under Royal Charter of Queen Elizabeth I. There was no permanent population, however, and Gilbert was lost at sea during his return voyage, thereby ending any immediate plans for settlement.

source.label: Wikipedia: St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador

history.text: With respect to the oldest surviving permanent English settlements in North America, it was preceded by Jamestown, Virginia (1607), the Cuper's Cove colony at Cupids in Newfoundland (1610), St. George's, Bermuda (1612), and the Bristol's Hope colony at Harbour Grace in Newfoundland (1618).

source.label: Wikipedia: St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador

history.text: The English government planned to expand these fortifications (Fort William) in around 1689, but construction did not begin until after the French admiral Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville captured and destroyed the town in the Avalon Peninsula Campaign (1696).

source.label: Wikipedia: St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador

history.label: 1700s
history.text: In the late 1700s, Fort Amherst and Fort Waldegrave were built to defend the harbour entrance.

source.label: Wikipedia: St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador

history.text: St. John's was destroyed by major fires in 1816, 1817, 1819, 1846 and 1892, when each time a large part of the city was destroyed.

source.label: Wikipedia: St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador

history.text: The Knights of Columbus Hostel fire in December 1942 saw 99 military and civilian lives lost.

source.label: Wikipedia: St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador

history.text: In July 2005, the flight was duplicated by American aviator and adventurer Steve Fossett in a replica Vickers Vimy aircraft, with St. John's International Airport substituting for Lester's Field (now an urban and residential part of the city).

source.label: Wikipedia: St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador
